# Entity Blindness in LLMs: Why ChatGPT Ignores Your Schema Markup (And What Actually Works)

## Introduction

If you’ve been investing time in schema markup because “structured data = better visibility,” you’re not alone — and you’re probably confused. Marketers, SEOs, and product teams have long relied on Schema.org JSON‑LD to communicate site structure to search engines. But with the rise of generative search and large language models (LLMs) like ChatGPT, many practitioners are discovering an uncomfortable truth: adding schema doesn’t reliably make your content show up in AI-generated answers. In some tests, LLMs simply ignore structured data unless the same information is present in visible text.

This article takes a tech-first look at why that happens (the tokenization problem), surveys real-world experiments and platform statements, and shows how to optimize for ranking on LLM-driven results — not just classic search. We’ll weave in published tests by practitioners like Mark Williams‑Cook and Julio C. Guevara, Microsoft’s March 2025 confirmation that Bing leverages schema, and a 2024 academic study demonstrating that GPT models can generate schema. If you care about generative search ranking, ChatGPT SEO, or entity optimization for LLMs, this guide will give you a pragmatic roadmap for what actually moves the needle.

Expect a technical but conversational analysis: how LLMs see web content, where structured data helps and where it doesn’t, what platforms such as Bing/Copilot are doing differently, and practical tactics you can deploy today to improve your chances of being cited in AI responses. At the end you’ll have actionable takeaways you can implement immediately and a solid mental model of how schema fits into the broader entity optimization puzzle.

## Understanding Entity Blindness in LLMs

The phrase “entity blindness” refers to an LLM’s inability — under certain conditions — to treat entities encoded in structured data (JSON‑LD schema, microdata, RDFa) as distinct, machine‑readable objects during retrieval and answer generation. Two mechanics cause this: how LLMs are trained (tokenization and context windows) and how retrieval/inference pipelines are implemented by platform providers.

Tokenization is the first, core problem. LLMs break input into tokens — the subword or byte sequences the model uses to learn and predict text. Mark Williams‑Cook’s experiments show that when content containing schema is tokenized, the structural relationships (for example, JSON‑LD keys like "@type": "Organization") are turned into sequences that are indistinguishable from ordinary token strings. The model remembers phrases and token probabilities, not the JSON object graph. That means schema in training corpora contributes only to token likelihoods rather than forming durable structured knowledge graphs the model can query directly.

Julio C. Guevara’s 2025 tests illustrate the practical fallout. He created two near‑identical product pages for contrived products that a model hadn’t seen before. One page presented product attributes as visible HTML text plus structured data; the other had only structured data with no visible text. When testers asked extraction prompts (price, SKU, color, etc.), the LLMs could retrieve attributes from the page with visible text but failed when information existed only in structured data. That’s a clear sign: typical LLMs, in inference, don’t reliably extract data that lives solely inside JSON‑LD.

But there’s a critical caveat: platform differences. In March 2025 Fabrice Canel from Microsoft publicly confirmed that schema markup helps Microsoft’s LLMs. That indicates Bing/Copilot uses structured data differently — likely via dedicated parsing and retrieval layers separate from the base LLM token stream. In other words, schema matters when a platform explicitly parses it at inference time and supplies it to the answer generation pipeline (or uses it to build or extend a knowledge graph used for retrieval).

Finally, academic work shows capability exists at the model level. A 2024 study on LLM4Schema.org found GPT‑3.5 and GPT‑4 can generate proper schema markup. That demonstrates models understand schema syntax and semantics sufficiently to produce it — but understanding/producing schema is not the same as systematically using schema for retrieval or ranking across platforms.

So why does ChatGPT “ignore” schema? Because off‑the‑shelf LLM inference (like using a vanilla generative model on web text) often relies on token-based context and retrieval mechanisms that do not preserve structural relationships from JSON‑LD. Without a retrieval layer that specifically extracts and wires structured data into the knowledge context, schema becomes one more chunk of tokenized text rather than an indexed entity graph.

## Key Components and Analysis

To optimize for generative search ranking and entity recognition in LLM environments, you need to understand five interlocking components: tokenization and training data, retrieval augmentation and index design, entity graphs and knowledge bases, UI-level citations (how bots source answers), and platform-specific parsing. Let’s break each down and show how they interact.

1. Tokenization and training data
- LLMs learn from huge text corpora tokenized into subword units. JSON strings and markup are tokenized just like prose; structural semantics are not automatically preserved as first-class graph relationships. This is why Mark Williams‑Cook’s experiments show schema “falling apart” during tokenization.
- Implication: Schema in raw crawled data contributes weakly to the underlying model’s internal representations unless converted into a separate structured knowledge format during training.

2. Retrieval augmentation and index design
- Modern LLM-based systems that answer queries at scale typically use a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) approach. RAG combines a retriever (vector or keyword index) with an LLM to supply relevant context for generation.
- If your structured data is parsed and indexed as fielded attributes or converted into vectorized representations, the retriever can surface those attributes to the model. If not, the structured data stays hidden.
- Microsoft’s public statements imply Bing/Copilot includes structured data parsing in its retrieval pipeline, whereas other services may not.

3. Entity graphs and knowledge bases
- Schema.org’s greatest value in an AI world is as a bridge into entity graphs (Knowledge Graphs) — machine‑readable nodes and relationships that retrieval systems can query directly.
- The sameAs field and consistent identifiers (Wikipedia, Wikidata, official profiles) are essential for tying pages to broader entity nodes. When platforms use entity graphs at inference, schema can be the nudge that connects your page to an established node.

4. UI-level sourcing and citation behavior
- Generative search engines often favor sources that provide clear, factual snippets (opening hours, prices, product specs) and will cite them in their answer or in an accompanying “sources” list.
- If the platform can parse schema and trust it, schema fields like openingHours or price can be displayed or used directly in outputs. If it can’t, the model falls back to visible text or external listings.

5. Platform-specific parsing and policy
- Microsoft’s March 2025 confirmation is a turning point: not all platforms treat schema the same. Bing’s LLMs incorporate structured data into their pipeline, while ChatGPT/Perplexity might not routinely parse external JSON‑LD when it makes answers.
- Practical takeaway: platform variance matters a lot. Optimization must account for which platforms you care about and how they ingest data.

Synthesis: The data from experiments (Williams‑Cook, Guevara) and the Microsoft confirmation intersect to form a clear technical thesis: schema is not inherently useless, but its effectiveness depends on whether the platform turns that structured markup into an indexed, retrievable signal rather than letting it be swallowed by tokenization. The 2024 LLM4Schema.org findings add nuance: models *can* understand and produce schema, which means the capability is present; adoption depends on pipeline design choices by platform engineers.

## Practical Applications

If your KPI is generative search ranking or being cited by an LLM-powered assistant, here’s a prioritized, tech‑savvy playbook that respects the limits demonstrated by testing while exploiting the places where schema helps.

1. Make content visible AND structured (mandatory)
- The Julio C. Guevara experiment shows schema-only pages fail extraction tests. Always publish the same facts as human-readable HTML plus JSON‑LD.
- Ensure prices, SKUs, product attributes, opening hours, and key facts are both in visible markup (structured HTML) and duplicated in JSON‑LD. Don’t hide essentials only in JSON‑LD.

2. Build or link to entity signals
- Use schema fields that tie to external authority: sameAs, url, identifier, and links to Wikipedia/Wikidata/LinkedIn/Crunchbase. These help entity disambiguation and improve chances of being linked to platform knowledge graphs.
- For organizations, include Organization schema with the proper name, contact info, logo, and sameAs references. For people, use Person schema with affiliation, role, and verified profiles.

3. Fielded indexing-friendly schema usage
- Use schema in a fielded, predictable way so that parsers can extract values. For example, product.price, product.sku, product.offers.priceCurrency — follow Schema.org property patterns.
- Avoid exotic nested structures that parsers may skip. Keep it consistent.

4. Implement machine-friendly HTML as well
- Use semantic HTML (article, header, nav) and microdata or clear id/class conventions that make scraping straightforward. Many retrievers rely on DOM-aware extraction before they consult JSON‑LD.

5. Promote cross-source consistency
- Consistent naming conventions, addresses, and contact details across your site, Google Business Profile, Bing Places, and authoritative third-party directories reinforce entity signals.
- If you want your brand entity to be recognized, ensure third-party listings replicate your canonical data.

6. Monitor platform-specific guidance and signals
- Microsoft’s confirmation means Bing/Copilot will likely favor schema-aware sites. Monitor Bing Webmaster Tools and Copilot guidance for changes.
- Track whether platforms add structured data parsers or require certain properties for feature eligibility.

7. Use RAG-style internal systems for your own models
- If you run your own LLM-driven assistant, build a retrieval layer that parses JSON‑LD into structured fields or vectors. That gives you direct control and avoids tokenization loss.
- Index schema fields separately in your search index or vector store so your retriever can point to specific attributes.

8. Test with controlled experiments
- Mirror the Guevara experiment in your environment: create two identical content sets (visible text + schema vs schema-only) and measure extraction and citation by the platforms you target.
- Log failures and adapt quickly.

9. Don’t neglect canonical content quality
- High-quality visible content, topical depth, and explicit answers to likely user questions remain essential. Schema is an amplifier, not a substitute.

These applications emphasize a hybrid approach: visible, human-facing content coupled with structured markup, plus external signals that tie your pages to consistent entities across the web.

## Challenges and Solutions

Let’s be candid about the friction points you’ll face and practical ways to address them.

Challenge: Tokenization destroys schema semantics during training
Solution: Treat schema as an indexable input for retrieval rather than as model training magic. Platforms that parse schema at inference time avoid this problem. If you control the stack (RAG pipeline or your enterprise assistant), extract JSON‑LD into fielded indices and vectorize the values. This ensures the model receives the structured facts as context rather than tokenized noise.

Challenge: Platform variance — Bing says it uses schema, others don’t
Solution: Adopt a multi-platform strategy. Focus on getting schema right for Bing/Copilot if that’s a priority, but maintain visible factual content to be robust across ChatGPT, Perplexity, and other services. Track platform announcements — Microsoft’s March 2025 statement is a leading indicator of how platform policy can pivot industry behavior.

Challenge: Schema-only pages fail in extraction tests
Solution: Duplicate critical facts in visible HTML. When you publish a product page, make sure the price, SKU, variants, and unique identifiers are present in the main content. Use structured data as an authoritative metadata layer, not the only copy.

Challenge: Trust and provenance for AI citations
Solution: Strengthen authoritative signals: canonical pages, verified pages, and sameAs links to trusted sources. Encourage third-party citations and authoritative backlinks; knowledge graphs love corroborated facts.

Challenge: Complexity in maintaining schema at scale
Solution: Automate schema generation from CMS or back-end product catalogs. Use canonical templates and validation (Schema.org validators, rich results tests). For large catalogs, parse and index schema values into a searchable vector store so retrievers surface up-to-date facts.

Challenge: SEO teams and engineering teams misaligned
Solution: Create shared contracts for structured data: engineering owns parsers and index workflows; SEO owns property mapping and content strategy. Use tests to prove value (A/B experiments showing increases in AI citations or traffic from generative sources).

Challenge: How to measure success
Solution: Build tracking systems that correlate page-level schema, visible content, and AI citations. Monitor mentions in generative engines where possible, use log analysis for bot access patterns, and employ synthetic tests asking known prompts to see which pages get surfaced.

These solutions are practical and implementable. They shift the focus from believing schema is a silver bullet to engineering a pipeline and site architecture that converts structured markup into retrievable, trustworthy signals.

## Future Outlook

Where does this all go from here? There are technical and market forces that will shape how schema interacts with LLMs in the next few years.

1. More platforms will parse schema at inference
- Microsoft’s March 2025 confirmation normalizes the idea that schema is useful when parsed outside the model. Expect other platforms to invest in structured data parsing to improve factuality and ease of extracting exact attributes.

2. Schema will be a retrieval-first signal, not a training crutch
- The industry consensus will likely settle on schema as a retrieval/inference tool rather than a way to “teach” models. That shifts investment from HTML-only schema implementation toward building indexed entity graphs and fielded indices.

3. Standardization and richer entity linking
- We’ll see improved conventions for entity IDs, better use of persistent global identifiers (Wikidata IDs, canonical URIs), and possibly new schema vocabularies designed specifically for LLM retrieval (lightweight, fielded JSON for vectorization).

4. New tooling and validators for AI readiness
- Expect tools that validate schema against LLM retrieval needs: “Is this field easily indexable? Are these values normalized?” Publishers will have automated QA that checks both human-readability and machine-readiness.

5. Emergence of AI-specific schema guidelines from platforms
- Platforms may publish stricter property lists for AI answers (e.g., Bing requires price and availability fields in product schema to be parsed for product answers). Early adopters will have an advantage.

6. Hybrid architectures will dominate
- RAG pipelines that combine vector search with structured fielded retrieval will be the norm. Enterprises that can parse JSON‑LD into both vectors and fielded stores will see the best results in internal assistant use cases and when syndicating content externally.

7. SEO evolves into entity optimization
- The hot skill will be “entity optimization for LLMs.” That means aligning content, structured data, cross‑platform identity, and real-world corroboration (listings, citations) to present a cohesive machine-readable identity.

8. Ethical and provenance concerns shape schema use
- Platforms will prefer authoritative, verifiable markup. False or manipulated structured data could be penalized or ignored, and provenance labels might become part of structured feeds.

In short: schema’s long-run future is strong, but it will be judged by how well it integrates with retrieval and entity systems, not by whether it sneaks facts into an LLM’s latent weights.

## Conclusion

Entity blindness in LLMs isn’t a complete refusal to use structured data — it’s a consequence of how models are trained, how platforms design inference pipelines, and how retrieval systems index content. Mark Williams‑Cook’s tokenization observations and Julio C. Guevara’s extraction tests make a clear point: schema-only content is insufficient. Microsoft’s March 2025 confirmation that Bing parses schema shows platform-level parsing changes the calculus. The 2024 academic work that GPT models can generate schema underscores that capability exists; the gap is engineering and pipeline design.

For practitioners focused on ranking on LLM results, the practical posture is clear: do everything right. Publish high-quality visible content, add robust and consistent JSON‑LD, tie pages to external authoritative identifiers, and ensure your structured data is parsed and indexed by the platforms you care about. If you operate your own LLM or RAG pipeline, extract JSON‑LD into both fielded indices and vector stores so the model gets crisp, retrievable facts. Monitor platform guidance and run controlled experiments to prove value.

Actionable takeaways:
- Always duplicate critical facts in visible HTML and JSON‑LD.
- Use sameAs and authoritative identifiers (Wikipedia/Wikidata) to connect to entity graphs.
- Parse and index schema server-side into fielded and vector stores for retrievers.
- Prioritize platforms: optimize for Bing/Copilot where schema is formally recognized, but remain robust across other LLMs.
- Automate schema generation and validation from canonical source-of-truth systems.

If you approach schema as part of a retrieval and entity strategy rather than a magic training input, you’ll move from being ignored to being cited. That’s how you win in the era of generative search ranking: make your entities visible, verifiable, and retrievable.
